title: Kenford Co. v. County of Erie
summary: The county’s knowledge that a stadium would increase surrounding land values did not establish that it assumed liability for Kenford’s lost appreciation if the stadium was never built.
notes: The editors emphasize that the tacit-agreement test has not generally been accepted and that UCC § 2-715 Comment 2 rejects it. The earlier refusal of the operator’s twenty-year profits involved both contemplation and reasonable certainty; that was a distinct claim from the land-appreciation award at issue here.

sections.Parties: Kenford Company owned or acquired land around a proposed stadium site. Dome Stadium, Inc. was the associated prospective operator. Erie County was the public contracting party whose failure to build the stadium generated the damages litigation.
sections.Material Facts:
The county planned a domed stadium, authorized $50 million in financing, and contracted with Kenford and the proposed operator. Kenford would donate 178 acres, and the county would begin construction and negotiate a forty-year lease; an agreed twenty-year management arrangement would operate if the lease negotiations failed. Projected revenues included taxes arising from expected appreciation of surrounding land. Kenford’s principal also acquired additional land nearby in anticipation of the development.

The anticipated project cost rose to approximately $72 million, and the county abandoned the transaction. Kenford sought both reliance losses and appreciation it said its peripheral land would have gained. The contract did not require Kenford to acquire or retain that peripheral land and did not promise to make good its appreciation if construction failed.
sections.Procedural History: An earlier trial produced several damages awards. Earlier appellate proceedings separately rejected the operator’s long-term lost profits and ordered a new trial on Kenford’s land-appreciation claim. That retrial produced a $6.5 million award, affirmed by the Appellate Division. In the 1989 decision excerpted here, the New York Court of Appeals reversed and struck the land-appreciation award. This disposition should not be confused with the earlier, separate treatment of reliance expenses or the operator’s profits.
sections.Issue: Did the parties contemplate responsibility for the owner’s lost appreciation in surrounding property as a recoverable consequence of the county’s breach?
sections.Holding: No. The record did not establish that the county assumed contractual responsibility for the anticipated appreciation. Awareness of the expected economic boom and of Kenford’s purchases was insufficient.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished an expectation that performance would bring a benefit from an understanding that the promisor would insure that benefit against nonperformance. The agreement described tax revenues expected from peripheral development, but this did not establish a guarantee of the owner’s hoped-for increase in land value. Nor did the record otherwise show an assumption of that large exposure.

Kenford acquired the surrounding property voluntarily. The county had not required that investment as its counterperformance, and the contract’s default arrangements did not contemplate the asserted liability. The court therefore treated the unrealized appreciation as a risk Kenford had retained. Its inquiry into the nature, purpose, and circumstances of the bargain draws on the assumption-of-responsibility or tacit-agreement approach to extraordinary damages.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Kenford makes it necessary to ask what risk the defendant assumed, rather than infer responsibility from bare knowledge of possible gain. It belongs beside Hadley and the contrasting Article 2 discussion.

topics.remedies: Rejects a particular extraordinary damages claim rather than all compensation for the stadium breach.
topics.foreseeability: Separates knowledge of hoped-for gains from assumed liability for their loss.
topics.risk-allocation: Uses the contract and surrounding circumstances to identify the risk retained by Kenford.
